Characterization of Vaginal Microbial Community Dynamics in the Pathogenesis of Incident Bacterial Vaginosis, a Pilot Study

## Abstract

Background: Despite over 60 years of research, the etiology of bacterial vaginosis (BV) remains controversial. In this pilot study, we utilized shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize vaginal microbial community changes prior to the development of incident BV (iBV).

Methods: A cohort of African American women with a baseline healthy vaginal microbiome (no Amsel Criteria, Nugent Score 0–3 with no Gardnerella vaginalis morphotypes) were followed for 90 days with daily self-collected vaginal specimens for iBV (≥2 consecutive days of a Nugent score of 7–10). Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on select vaginal specimens from 4 women, every other day for 12 days prior to iBV diagnosis. Sequencing data were analyzed through Kraken2 and bioBakery 3 workflows, and specimens were classified into community state types (CSTs). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed to compare the correlation of read counts to bacterial abundance.

Results: Common BV-associated bacteria such as G. vaginalis, Prevotella bivia, and Fannyhessea vaginae were increasingly identified in the participants prior to iBV. Linear modeling indicated

The Lactobacillus spp. decline correlated with the presence of Lactobacillus phages. We observed enrichment in bacterial adhesion factor genes on days prior to iBV. This pilot study characterizes the pathogenesis of bacterial vaginosis using shotgun metagenomic sequencing of longitudinal vaginal specimens from African American women.

## Introduction

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women,1 and this dysbiosis is strongly associated with adverse birth outcomes,2 pelvic inflammatory disease (PID),3 and increased risk of acquisition and transmission of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV.4–6 The prevalence of BV is higher among African American (AA) women (51.4%) compared to Caucasian women (23.2%),7 and the annual economic burden of prevalent BV is estimated to be 4.8 billion US dollars.8 A large body of epidemiologic data suggest that BV is an STI, with a hypothesized incubation period of 4–7 days,9,10 but its exact etiology remains unknown.

Despite over 60 years of research, the specific mechanisms of incident BV (iBV) pathogenesis remain unclear. The vaginal microbiome of women with BV is characterized by reduced numbers of lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli and dramatically increased numbers of facultative and strict anaerobic BV-associated bacteria (BVAB), including Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella spp., Fannyhessea vaginae, and Megasphaera spp., compared to the vaginal microbiome of women without BV.6 It has been proposed that BVAB could be introduced via sexual transmission.11–13 Alternatively, the proliferation of BVAB could be triggered by the loss of protective vaginal Lactobacillus spp. due to menses, sexual activity, Lactobacillus phage, and/or other inciting factors.14–17

An interplay between these hypotheses could also be occurring, and sexual transmission of BVAB along with loss of protective lactobacilli could represent successive steps in developing BV.18

In our prior study, we characterized the vaginal microbiota of a cohort of AA women who have sex with women (WSW) over a 90 day period using daily self-collected vaginal specimens and 16S rRNA gene sequencing.19 We determined that the relative abundance of L. crispatus significantly decreased in participants who developed iBV (Nugent score 7–10 on ≥2 consecutive days) starting 14 days prior to diagnosis, compared to age and race-matched women who did not. Conversely, the relative abundance of several key BVAB significantly increased 3–4 days prior to the development of iBV (P. bivia, G. vaginalis) or on the day of iBV (F. vaginae, Megasphaera type I).19 As 16S rRNA gene sequencing only

Although 16S rRNA gene sequencing has provided critical insights into the composition of vaginal bacterial communities during health and disease,20 this approach has limitations, as mentioned above. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing provides a more comprehensive insight into the composition of the vaginal microbiota, including genomic and functional data on all bacterial and non-bacterial DNA present in the vaginal micro-environment.20 It can often yield a finer phylogenetic resolution of the bacterial taxa and, we hypothesize, a more accurate measurement of absolute abundance.

In this study, we analyzed longitudinal vaginal specimens from a subset of AA WSW who developed iBV from our prior study using shotgun metagenomic sequencing to further study changes in the vaginal microbiota prior to iBV to better understand its pathogenesis.

## Materials and Methods

Study Population and Sampling

This sub-study and the parent study were approved by the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB) Institutional Review Board (IRB) (Protocol F131127001),19 the Jefferson County Department of Health (JCDH) Research Review Committee (Protocol 2015–03), and the Louisiana State University IRB (Protocol 8738). This study was exempt by the Indiana University (IU) IRB. In the parent study, 42 AA non-pregnant WSW with baseline normal vaginal microbiota (no Amsel criteria21 and a normal Nugent score22 of 0–3 with no G. vaginalis morphotypes), no oral or intra-vaginal antibiotic use within the past 14 days, and no current STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis) were enrolled at the JCDH Sexual Health Clinic in Birmingham, Alabama.19 These women provided daily selfcollected vaginal specimens for 90 days or until the development of iBV (Nugent score 7–10 on ≥2 consecutive days). Participants completed a study enrollment questionnaire to obtain socio-demographic information as well as medical and sexual history data. Participants also filled out daily diaries about their sexual partners and menses throughout the study period.19

Based on previous 16S rRNA gene sequencing (Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content 2.pdf. Heatmap of 16S rRNA gene sequencing from the four participants),19 we selected a subset of stored vaginal specimens from 4 participants who developed iBV for the purposes of this pilot study. We selected specimens from the first day of iBV diagnosis (day 0), along with every other day for the 10 days prior to iBV (days −2 to −10). If a vaginal specimen was unavailable (i.e., day −8 for K12), the next available specimen closest in time was chosen.

Shotgun Metagenomic Sequencing

DNA was isolated, as previously described,19 sent to the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at IU, and prepared for shotgun metagenomic sequencing. The NexteraXT library prep kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA) was used, and samples were paired-end sequenced (2 × 150 bp) on a HiSeq4000. Raw fastq files were used for bioinformatics analysis. Sequences were deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (PRJNA707585)

Taxonomic Assignment and Processing

We used multiple processing and classification tools to rigorously classify and analyze the sequence reads from this pilot study. First, Kraken2 v2.0.9-beta was used to map the sequences against the MaxiKraken database (Loman Lab, https://lomanlab.github.io/ mockcommunity/mc_databases.html).23 Organisms assigned less than 10 reads by Kraken2, and potential reagent contaminants were removed from further analysis (Table S1B, Supplemental Digital Content 1, Contamination Removal). Following analysis with Kraken2, further analysis was carried out using the bioBakery 3 suite of tools.24 VIRGO was used as a third method for taxonomic classification.25 Relative abundance was obtained by dividing each microorganism’s read count by the total read count in each specimen to adjust for sequencing variation. Maximal reads were chosen due to the hypothesized significant increase in bacterial reads on the day of iBV that may skew filtering if averaging was performed.6,11

Metagenomic Bacterial Analysis

Bacterial strain composition was determined using Panphlan 3.0 to map shotgun reads to species pangenomes and reference strain gene sets.26 Bray-Curtis dissimilarity distances were calculated from gene sets generated from Panphlan 3. Results were visualized using Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) and clustered using k-means. KEGG overrepresentation analysis and virulence factor (VF) identification was performed using cluster profiler 4.0 and ShortBRED respectively.27,28 CSTs were determined with VALENCIA.29

Metagenomic Phage Analysis

To investigate Lactobacillus phage origin and activity as part of this analysis, we performed metagenomic assembly using the ATLAS workflow and phage contigs were identified using VIBRANT.30,31s Further details of these methods are described in Supplemental Digital Content 9.pdf.

Bacterial Abundance Measurement

We used quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays to compare the correlation between sequence reads and bacterial abundance. The proportion of bacterial reads to total reads was compared to the total bacterial load (16S rRNA copy number) using universal V6 primers, as described.32s Based on their predominant relative abundance in our samples, we compared the log-scaled relative abundance of G. vaginalis and Lactobacillus spp. from Kraken2, Metaphlan 3, and VIRGO to their 16S copy numbers using specific V6 primers. Additional qPCR information is listed in (Table S1C, Supplemental Digital Content 1, qPCR information).

Statistical Analysis

All visualizations were generated in R v4.2.1 using the package ggplot2.33,34s Statistical analysis used the R package MaAslin2,35s which specializes in multivariable associations in

## Results

Characteristics of the Study Population

Basic demographic, sexual history, and tobacco use data for the 4 participants with iBV included in this sub-study (K12, K18, K19, K20) are listed in Table 1. A total of 24 vaginal specimens from these 4 participants were sequenced (6 specimens/woman). Fig 1A indicates relevant metadata for each woman, along with an indication of which days were sequenced via 16S rRNA gene sequencing in the parent study and shotgun metagenomic sequencing in this pilot study.19

Microbial Composition of the Vaginal Specimens

Over 85% of the shotgun metagenomic sequences were human; bacteria accounted for most non-human sequences (Fig 1B). There was a significant increase in reads originating from bacterial micro-organisms on the day of iBV in 3 of the 4 women, with most of the remaining sequences corresponding to fungi (Fig 1C). The distribution of viral sequences is displayed in Fig 1D. An increase in viral reads occurred in K20 corresponding to human gammaherpesvirus 4 (Epstein Barr Virus) prior to iBV, which may be a marker of cellular infiltrate (B cells).37s Overall, we found more precise assignment of species using shotgun metagenomic sequencing compared to our previous 16S analysis (Figure S2, Supplemental Digital Content 3.pdf. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics taxonomic comparison).19

Ordination of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity distances from sample species relative abundance reflect the microbial community dynamics occurring during the onset of iBV for each participant (Fig 1E). The difference in Bray-Curtis distance between consecutively collected samples is plotted in (Figure S3A, Supplemental Digital Content 4.pdf, Comparisons of distances between longitudinal specimens). CST categorization and scores are reported in (Table S1D, Supplemental Digital Content 1, CST scores). In 3 of the 4 participants sampled, the greatest change in distance occurred in communities labeled as CST III, L. iners, dominated communities. This observation aligns with previous findings suggesting L. iners communities are transitional.38s

The most abundant micro-organisms are displayed in heatmaps (Fig 2A, B), ordered by maximum read count across all samples. Analysis with Kraken2 (Fig 2A) revealed that the highest overall relative abundance was attributed to G. vaginalis, F. vaginae, and P. bivia on the day of iBV. Taxonomic classification using the vaginal microbiome specific taxonomic classification tool VIRGO (Figure S4, Supplemental Digital Content 5.pdf. Taxonomic analysis using VIRGO) generated similar results to Metaphlan 3.0 (Fig 2B), however

a greater relative abundance was attributed to Lactobacillus spp. Overall, bacterial taxa detected prior to and on the day of iBV matched previously reported findings.19

The relative abundance of several common BVAB increased leading up to iBV while Lactobacillus spp. declined. To confirm this observation, we generated linear models correlating Nugent Scores and temporal metrics to species relative abundance using MaAslin2 (Figure S5A, Supplemental Digital Content 6.pdf, B. MaAslin2 results, Table S1E, Supplemental Digital Content 1, MaAslin2 results). We found statistically significant associations with F. vaginae (P=0.04) and G. vaginalis (P=0.07) relative abundance increasing as day of iBV approached. P. bivia relative abundance significantly increased prior to iBV (P=0.08) in subject K18 using linear models. We also found significant decreases in the relative abundance of L. iners (P=0.09), L. crispatus (P=0.01), and L. jensenii (P=0.07) across all specimens as well as L. gasseri (P=0.08) in K18 on days leading up to iBV. When categorizing Nugent scores as low (0–3), intermediate (4–6), and high (7–10), we found that the relative abundance of F. vaginae was only >1% on days of high Nugent scores, suggesting that it functions as a mediator of iBV later in onset.11

Functional annotations prior to iBV

Functional annotations were performed using HUMAnN 3.0 (Fig 3A). Samples were clustered by CST. The pathway with the highest relative abundance on the day of iBV was the glycogen degradation II pathway. The relative abundance of this pathway was found to be significantly higher on the day of iBV compared to days leading up to iBV (P=0.01). G. vaginalis was found to be the principal contributor to this pathway (Table S1F, Supplemental Digital Content 1, Species contributions to pathways).39s Additionally, the pathway 5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide biosynthesis was significantly enriched in samples with iBV CST compared to type I and III CSTs (P=0.01).

To further assess functional changes, reads were mapped to virulence factor (VF) libraries. L. iners and G. vaginalis specific VFs, inerolysin and vaginolysin respectively, showed unique gene abundance patterns, which closely mirrored the relative abundance of each species. Additionally, genes associated with chaperones and adhesion proteins were more abundant in samples leading up to the day of iBV.40,41s This was particularly clear in samples from participant K19. Row normalized VF abundance is shown in (Figure S3B, Supplemental Digital Content 4.pdf. Heatmap of virulence factor abundance).

G. vaginalis is thought to exist in both commensal and pathogenic clades, as it is detected in women with and without BV.42s To better characterize G. vaginalis in the development of iBV, we investigated the genetic composition of strains found in our specimens. G. vaginalis strains were identified in 19 of 24 samples. Strain similarity was visualized using a PCoA plot (Fig 3B). The dominant strain of G. vaginalis in 15 of the 19 samples clustered with reference genomes associated with strains previously identified to be from clade 1.43s

Despite identifying strains from multiple clades, we did not find a difference in strain pathway enrichment on days leading up to iBV compared to the day of iBV.

Lactobacillus phages in iBV pathogenesis

We sought to better characterize the bacteriophage population due to the presence of phages in some quantity in all participants prior to iBV (Fig 1D). While phage reads made up a small proportion of total microbial reads, they made up a larger proportion of viral reads (~10%). Analysis with VIBRANT indicated that the majority of the assembled Lactobacillus phage contigs did not also contain bacterial DNA (Fig S6, Table S1G, Supplemental Digital Content 7.pdf, Lactobacillus phage results).31s The total Lactobacillus phage relative abundance decreased leading up to iBV (P=0.01) (Figure S7, Supplemental Digital Content 6.pdf, Fig S5C. MaAslin2 results, Table S1E, Supplemental Digital Content 1, MaAslin2 results). Additionally, total Lactobacillus phage relative abundance positively correlated with L. crispatus (P=0.09), and both decreased prior to iBV (Fig 4). Phage contig coverage was found to be significantly higher than associated host Lactobacillus coverage in 6 samples on days leading up to iBV (P<0.01), indicating that Lactobacillus phages could be active in these samples (Table S1J, Supplemental Digital Content 1, Phage coverage and activity).

Estimating abundance using qPCR

The ratio of bacterial reads to total sequencing reads was hypothesized to be an estimate of absolute bacterial abundance in the specimens.44s The estimated abundance of bacterial reads increased on the day of iBV for all 4 participants (Fig 2B). In 3 of the 4 participants (K12, K18, K19), this increase was over 10-fold compared to the prior five vaginal specimens. The fourth participant, K20, showed a nearly 2-fold increase on the day of iBV. To verify that these reads could estimate absolute abundance, qPCR assays measuring total bacterial load (16S rRNA copy number), as well as G. vaginalis and Lactobacillus spp., were performed. V6 specific 16S rRNA copy numbers were compared to the corresponding read counts from Kraken2, Metaphlan 3, and VIRGO using MaAslin2 (Figure S5D, Supplemental Digital Content 6.pdf. MaAslin2 results, see Table S1E, Supplemental Digital Content 1). We observed a strong correlation between the total bacterial load to the proportion of bacterial reads to total sequenced reads (including human reads, P=0.001). Comparing the qPCR-derived copies to read counts for Lactobacillus spp. and G. vaginalis, we observed the strongest correlation using Kraken2 (P=4E-9, 1.5E-5) followed by Metaphlan 3 (P=1E-6, 7E-4), and VIRGO (P=0.05, 0.04). Overall, these results indicate that estimations of bacterial absolute abundance can be made based on the ratio of bacterial to total sequencing reads.

## Discussion

Discovering the etiology of iBV remains an active area of research, and the causal pathway leading to iBV is yet to be identified.11,12,45s It is unknown whether vaginal lactobacilli decrease first in iBV pathogenesis, allowing BVAB to proliferate, or whether BVAB are introduced first, suppressing vaginal lactobacilli.11 Various factors leading to the depletion of vaginal Lactobacillus spp. in iBV pathogenesis have been studied, including but not limited to douching,46s spermicides (e.g., Nonoxynol-9),47s and Lactobacillus phages.14–17

Our findings in this pilot study indicate G. vaginalis increases in relative abundance on days leading up to iBV, while F. vaginae increases in relative abundance on the day of iBV. There are data that P. bivia is involved in the early stages of BV biofilm formation and iBV pathogenesis.11,19,48s,49s Although P. bivia was observed in all participants in some quantity in this study, we observed a significant association between P. bivia abundance and iBV onset in only 1 of the 4 participants. This finding may be due to the small sample size of this study, limiting the ability to identify exact changes in bacterial abundance; future studies should include larger sample sizes. Additionally, results of this study support the notion that L. iners-dominated communities are less resistant to rapid transitions.38s

Analysis of functional annotations showed enrichment in adhesion-related genes on days leading up to iBV. It is hypothesized that adhesion of G. vaginalis to the vaginal epithelium is the first step in BV biofilm formation.11 This finding may reflect an increased abundance of genes involved in cell adhesion on days prior to iBV. Identifying adhesion proteins which accumulate prior to iBV could be important in determining proteins contributing to the pathogenesis of G. vaginalis. Additionally, we observed an enrichment in glycogen degradation genes copies associated with G. vaginalis, including on the day of iBV, reflecting the macromolecules utilized at the time of iBV.

We identified Lactobacillus phages as far as 10 days prior to iBV in all 4 of the participants in this study. These phages correlated with a decrease in protective Lactobacillus spp.50s A depletion of protective Lactobacillus spp. by phages may play a role in the pathogenesis of iBV, although this requires further study.15 Lactobacillus phage phi jlb1 and KC5a are reported to target L. gasseri in vitro,51s,52s while Lactobacillus phage Lv-1 has been found to target L. jensenii in the vaginal exudate of a healthy, reproductive-age woman.53s Phages targeting L. crispatus have been challenging to delineate as historical studies were performed on L. acidophilus (targeted by KC5A), which was later reclassified into multiple species, including L. crispatus.54s A prior study of vaginal specimens from 39 reproductive-age women identified 7 Lactobacillus phages from 37 Lactobacillus strains isolated from 27 women (19 with normal vaginal flora and 8 with BV based on Amsel criteria).14 The rate of phage isolation was much lower in healthy women than in women with BV. Interestingly, phage фkc039, while lysogenic in one woman in which it was isolated from, was able to lyse lactobacilli in other women in this study. While we did find enrichment in phage DNA compared to host DNA on days leading up to iBV, evidence that these phages could be lytic, although in vivo experiments will be needed to validate these findings. Additional studies on the potential role of sexual transmission of infectious Lactobacillus phages in iBV pathogenesis are needed.15

Strengths of this pilot study include increased resolution of taxonomic classifications for bacterial micro-organisms compared to 16S rRNA gene sequencing and characterization of vaginal micro-organisms longitudinally in a unique group of women with iBV. We utilized three widely used tools for shotgun metagenomic sequencing, Kraken2,23 bioBakery 3,24 and specifically for the vaginal microbiome, VIRGO.25 Additionally, we have shown that shotgun metagenomic sequencing estimates absolute bacterial abundance based on the proportion of bacterial to total sequencing reads; these results remained accurate for specific vaginal bacteria, G. vaginalis and Lactobacillus spp.44s

Despite these strengths, this study has limitations. The cost of shotgun metagenomic sequencing is substantially higher than 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Thus, we only sequenced four participants resulting in our study being underpowered. Although we carried out statistical testing and found statistically significant differences, these findings can only estimate clinical significance. Additionally, we were only able to sequence a smaller number of specimens (n=24) over a limited time period (every other day for the 10 days prior to iBV) than in our prior 16S study.19 There could have been important changes occurring in the intervening days that we may have missed in this analysis. We also did not sequence specimens from participants who did not develop iBV to compare them to iBV women; this is an area of future research as we have stored specimens from control participants. Additionally, the participants included in this study were AA WSW presenting to a Sexual Health Clinic in the Southern US, making it difficult to generalize these results to all women. However, BV is highly prevalent among this population, and this study could lead to targeted efforts to optimize sexual health in this community.52s,53s Also, phages (and other viruses) comprised only a small proportion of non-bacterial reads in this study (Fig 1C), perhaps due to the self-collected nature of the sampling technique, which might not pick up all organisms equally.55s Future studies could consider clinician-collected specimens however this may not be feasible on a daily basis. To address these limitations, future well-powered studies with larger sample sizes, appropriate controls, and more frequent sequencing are needed.

In conclusion, this pilot study proposes interactions between specific vaginal organisms in the development of iBV. The results should be further explored in larger cohorts of women with and without iBV.
